newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Progress aside, EU faults U.S. trade policy.
newsitem.headline: Progress aside, EU faults U.S. trade policy.

text.p: Tariffs, "Buy America" provisions and a U.S. proclivity for imposing rules on others are dogging EU-U.S. relations despite progress in pushing global liberalisation, the European Commission said on Tuesday.

In its annual report on U.S. trade barriers, the European Union's executive highlighted what it said was an "unwelcome new development" -- a tendency of U.S. states to impose limits on foreign firms that do business in countries with questionable human rights records.
It cited in particular a Massachusetts law restricting foreign companies with interests in Burma from state government procurement contracts.
"Quite apart for the strict legality of (such) actions, they are clearly disturbing the conduct of normal international economic relations," the Commission said in a statement.

The report was quick to note the positive in EU-U.S. relations, saying that a 1995 agreement to forge a new transatlantic partnership had become a powerful driving force for economic liberalisation across the world.
There had also been improvements since last year in opening the U.S. market to the professional services sector and some progress over intellectual property, the Commission said.
But the report otherwise carried a litany of complaints about the way U.S. law and policy restricts EU businesses.
Chief among the EU complaints was the trend towards extraterritoriality -- the imposition of U.S. foreign policy goals on non-U.S. businesses.
The most prominent examples have come at the federal level with the Helms-Burton law on Cuba and the D'Amato law on Libya and Iran.
Both laws seek to discourage non-U.S. companies from doing business with the countries concerned -- viewed as pariah nations by Washington -- by threatening various restrictions on the companies.
The EU has been vociferous in its condemnation of the laws, which are now effectively on hold as far as EU companies are concerned a result of diplomatic negotiations.
But in its report on Tuesday, the Commission was equally scathing about the growing trend of U.S. states to impose their political goals on non-U.S. companies.
As well as the Massachusetts Burma law, it noted that "selective purchasing laws" had been adopted in New York City and proposed in states such as California, Connecticut and Texas.

"The multiplication of such initiatives seems indicative of a worrying new trend in U.S. sub-federal policy-making aimed at regulating the behaviour of economic agents beyond U.S. territorial jurisdiction," the Commission said.

Regarding other barriers to trade, the Commission said that despite an overall decrease there were still significant tariffs in the textile, footwear, leather good, jewellery, ceramics and glass sectors.
U.S. states also set different standards from international norms, while "Buy America" provisions in various state and federal programmes remained a cause for EU concern.
The U.S. embassy in Brussels was not immediately available for comment on the report.
